passages.t: A Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year
passages.happening:
“These are the ordinances that you are to set before them” (verse 1).

“If you buy a Hebrew servant, he is to serve you for six years. But in the seventh year, he shall go free without paying anything” (verse 2). If he came with a wife, she leaves with him (verse 3). If his master gave him a wife and they had children, the wife and children stay with the master, and the man goes free alone (verse 4).

But the servant may choose to stay: “I love my master and my wife and children; I do not want to go free” (verse 5). Then the master brings him before the judges, pierces his ear with an awl at the door or doorpost, “Then he shall serve his master for life” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The people asked Moses to hear God's words for them (20:19), and from here he does. Chapters 21 to 23 are called the Book of the Covenant, after the scroll Moses reads aloud in 24:7. The Ten Commandments gave the principles. These chapters show them at work in village life: debt, family, fights, animals, land and courts.

It helps to know what kind of law this is. It is case law. Each law begins with ‘if’: if this happens, then this is the ruling. It does not try to cover every case. It sets out typical cases, so that judges could learn to reason from them to cases that were not written down. The word ‘ordinances’ in verse 1 is mishpatim, rulings for judges, from the Hebrew word for justice.

Israel was not the first people to write laws like these. The best known older collection is the law of Hammurabi, king of Babylon, carved on a stone pillar around 1750 BC and found at Susa in 1901. It too deals with debt servants, fights, a pregnant woman struck in a quarrel, and an ox that gores. Israel's law spoke the legal language of its world. But the differences are as telling as the likenesses. Hammurabi's penalties change with the victim's rank. Israel's law comes as the word of God to the whole people, not the decree of a king, and it keeps giving a reason drawn from memory: you were slaves in Egypt.

How do Christians relate to these laws? In more than one way. Many, following Thomas Aquinas, Calvin and the Westminster Confession, divide the law of Moses into moral, ceremonial and civil laws: the moral law still binds, the sacrifices are fulfilled in Christ, and Israel's civil laws ended with Israel's state, though the justice behind them still teaches. Lutherans stress the difference between law, which shows sin, and gospel, which forgives. Dispensational and New Covenant readers hold that the covenant of Sinai as a whole ended with Christ, and that believers live under ‘the law of Christ’. These notes take no side among these readings. They read these laws first as what they were: justice for a people God had just set free.

Now the first case. It is about a slave's freedom. A people just come out of ‘the house of slavery’ (20:2) must write limits on servitude into their own law. Debt was the usual road into it. A family that lost a harvest might sell a son, a daughter, or itself to pay what it owed. The law does not abolish that. It caps it. Six years, and then freedom, ‘without paying anything’. The seventh year echoes the Sabbath just commanded (20:8-11).

The pierced ear is a public sign. A servant who chooses to stay, for love of his household, is marked at the doorpost before the judges. His choice is made in the open.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy restates the law and adds a gift: “when you release him, do not send him away empty-handed” (Deuteronomy 15:13). It gives the reason: “Remember that you were slaves in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God redeemed you” (Deuteronomy 15:15).

Leviticus goes further for a fellow Israelite who sells himself: “Let him stay with you as a hired worker or temporary resident” (Leviticus 25:40), and “You are not to rule over them harshly, but you shall fear your God” (Leviticus 25:43).

Centuries later the people of Jerusalem freed their Hebrew slaves and then took them back. Jeremiah condemned them, quoting this law: “Every seventh year, each of you must free his Hebrew brother who has sold himself to you” (Jeremiah 34:14).
passages.hard:
Why does God's law allow slavery at all, instead of forbidding it?

That question should be faced honestly, and these notes do not defend slavery.

Here is what the law permits. A person could be bought, and could work for another without wages to pay a debt. A wife given by the master stayed with the master when the man went free (verse 4), which could force a cruel choice between freedom and family. Other laws allowed foreigners to be held for life (Leviticus 25:44-46). That is in the text, and it cannot be explained away.

Here is what the law limits. A Hebrew servant goes free in the seventh year. Kidnapping a person is a crime punished by death (verse 16). A master who maims a servant loses him (verses 26-27). An escaped slave is not to be sent back (Deuteronomy 23:15-16). Hammurabi's law, by contrast, put to death the man who sheltered a runaway. Many readers, among them Christopher Wright, read these laws the way Jesus read the divorce law: Moses permitted it ‘because of your hardness of heart’ (Matthew 19:8). A law can limit a harm in a fallen society without calling the harm good. Critics answer that the laws still allowed one person to own another, and that this has to be faced. Both things are true to the text.

The history of these verses is painful. In the Atlantic slave trade and in the American South, slaveholders and many preachers used texts like these to defend slavery as biblical. That was a misuse, and it was wrong. Atlantic slavery, built on race and kidnapping, was very different from the debt service of these verses, and the law of Moses punished kidnapping with death. Christians who opposed slavery drew on the same Bible, on human dignity, the exodus and the gospel. The church's record was mixed, and it must be named honestly.

The site's guide to the slavery texts, and the Reading the Law guide, go further.
passages.asks: The first law given to a people just freed from slavery limits slavery among themselves. Ask how your own rescue by God shapes the way you treat people who have less power than you. And ask whom you hold in a debt, of money or of grievance, that it is time to release.

passages.t: A daughter sold as a servant
passages.happening:
“And if a man sells his daughter as a servant, she is not to go free as the menservants do” (verse 7).

“If she is displeasing in the eyes of her master who had designated her for himself, he must allow her to be redeemed. He has no right to sell her to foreigners, since he has broken faith with her” (verse 8).

“And if he chooses her for his son, he must deal with her as with a daughter” (verse 9). If he takes another wife, “he must not reduce the food, clothing, or marital rights of his first wife” (verse 10). If he does not give her these three things, “she is free to go without monetary payment” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Here a poor father sells his daughter. In that world it was usually done to pay a debt, and the girl was usually meant to become a wife of the master or of his son. That is why she does not leave after six years like a male servant. She was not being hired for a term. She was being given into a household as a wife.

Then the law turns to protect her. If the master changes his mind, he must let her family buy her back. He may not sell her to foreigners, because he ‘has broken faith with her’: the law names his rejection as a wrong done to her. If she is given to his son, she must be treated as a daughter of the house. If the master takes another wife, he may not cut her food, her clothing or her marital rights. And if he fails in any of these, she goes free, owing nothing.

These are limits on a man's power over a woman who had very little power of her own. Without such a law she could have been passed on, sold again, or left without support. This law says she may not be.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy's version of the release law names women as well as men: “If a fellow Hebrew, a man or a woman, is sold to you and serves you six years, then in the seventh year you must set him free” (Deuteronomy 15:12).

When Jerusalem's people took back the slaves they had freed, Jeremiah says they took back ‘the menservants and maidservants whom you had set at liberty’ (Jeremiah 34:16), and God called it a profaning of his name.

Paul named the trade in people among the deeds the law condemns: ‘for slave traders and liars and perjurers’ (1 Timothy 1:10).
passages.hard:
Why does God's law allow a father to sell his daughter?

This is one of the hardest laws in the book, and it should not be softened. The law assumes a world where a poor father could sell a girl to pay what he owed. It does not forbid the sale, and it does not ask what she wants. A modern reader is right to be troubled.

What the law does is limit what may be done to her once she is sold. She cannot be resold to strangers. She cannot be left without food, clothing or her rights as a wife. If the man who took her breaks faith with her, she goes free. In its own world, that was protection for someone who had almost none. It does not make the sale good. It shows a law pressing against the harm of its world without yet removing it.

These verses must never be used to treat a daughter, or any woman, as something a family may trade or a man may own.

A word for anyone who is being held, owned or forced to work today. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The law named the master's rejection of the girl a breaking of faith. Ask where people with little power are being passed from hand to hand around you, and what faithfulness to them would require. And ask whether you keep faith with those who depend on you when it costs you.

passages.t: Life for life, and a place to flee
passages.happening:
“Whoever strikes and kills a man must surely be put to death” (verse 12). But if he did not plan it, “but God allowed it to happen, then I will appoint for you a place where he may flee” (verse 13). If a man plots to kill his neighbor, “you must take him away from My altar to be put to death” (verse 14).

“Whoever strikes his father or mother must surely be put to death” (verse 15).

“Whoever kidnaps another man must be put to death, whether he sells him or the man is found in his possession” (verse 16).

“Anyone who curses his father or mother must surely be put to death” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
Now come the laws about life, each marked by the grave words ‘must surely be put to death’.

There were no police in ancient Israel. When someone was killed, a relative, called the avenger of blood, was expected to pursue the killer. Verse 13 limits that. A killing that was not planned, an accident or a sudden blow, is not treated like murder. God will name a place where the killer can flee. Later these became the cities of refuge. But a planned murder has no shelter, not even at God's altar. People who grasped the altar hoped the holy place would protect them. This law says it may not protect a murderer.

The law weighs intent. A planned killing and an accident are not the same, even when the result is the same.

Verse 16 makes kidnapping a crime punished by death, whether the person has already been sold or is still held. Stealing a human being is treated as an attack on life itself.

Verses 15 and 17 protect parents. Cursing a parent here does not mean a moment of rudeness. It meant rejecting one's parents, or calling down harm on them. The household was the foundation of the covenant people, and an attack on it was treated with great seriousness.

These penalties should be read soberly. They were the law of an ancient people under God, decided by judges and witnesses. They are not a pattern for anyone today to take into their own hands, and they give no one permission to harm a child who disobeys.
passages.later:
Numbers sets up the cities of refuge “so that a person who kills someone unintentionally may flee there” (Numbers 35:11), and forbids any payment to buy off a murderer: “You are not to accept a ransom for the life of a murderer who deserves to die” (Numbers 35:31).

When Joab, who had shed blood, fled to the altar, Solomon had him taken from it (1 Kings 2:28-34).

Jesus quotes verse 17 against teachers whose rules let a son avoid supporting his parents: “For God said, ‘Honor your father and mother’ and ‘Anyone who curses his father or mother must be put to death’” (Matthew 15:4).
passages.asks: The law draws a line between a planned wrong and an accident. Ask whether you judge others by what they meant, or only by what happened, and whether you judge yourself by the same rule. And ask where you have treated a person as something to be used or traded.

passages.happening:
If men quarrel and one strikes the other, and the injured man is laid up but recovers, the one who struck him goes unpunished, but “he must compensate the man for his lost work and see that he is completely healed” (verses 18-19).

“If a man strikes his manservant or maidservant with a rod, and the servant dies by his hand, he shall surely be punished” (verse 20).

“However, if the servant gets up after a day or two, the owner shall not be punished, since the servant is his property” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The first case is a fight between equals. The man who did the harm pays for the other's lost time and for his healing. The aim is to put things right, not to punish for its own sake.

Then a master strikes his servant. If the servant dies, the master ‘shall surely be punished’. The Hebrew word means the death is to be avenged. A slave's death was treated as a crime, not just the loss of property.

Verse 21 is harder. If the servant lives a day or two, the master is not punished, ‘since the servant is his property’. The Hebrew says, word for word, that the servant is ‘his silver’.
passages.later:
Job saw master and servant as made by one God: “Did not He who made me in the womb also make them? Did not the same One form us in the womb?” (Job 31:15). He knew that he would answer to God if he rejected their complaint (Job 31:13-14).

Paul told masters, “Give up your use of threats, because you know that He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no favoritism with Him” (Ephesians 6:9).
passages.hard:
How can the law call a servant property?

Readers rightly find verse 21 hard, and it should not be softened. It allows a master to beat a servant, and it calls the servant his silver.

Several things are said in reply. Verse 20 treats the killing of a servant as a crime to be avenged, which was unusual in its world. The lesser rule of verse 21 may reflect how hard it was to prove intent when death came later, with the loss of the servant's work as its own penalty. And a few verses on, a master who knocks out a servant's eye or tooth loses the servant (verses 26-27). Many interpreters read this law as restraining an evil in a fallen society, not approving it.

But none of this makes verse 21 comfortable, and it should not. In later centuries verses like this were used to defend slavery, including in the American South. That was a misuse, and it was wrong. No one may use these words to excuse harm done to any person.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The law made the man who did harm pay for the other's healing. Ask whom you have hurt and never helped to heal. And ask whether you ever speak of people under you as if they were only what they cost you or earn you.

passages.t: Harm to a pregnant woman, and ‘eye for eye’
passages.happening:
“If men who are fighting strike a pregnant woman and her child is born prematurely, but there is no further injury, he shall surely be fined as the woman’s husband demands and as the court allows” (verse 22).

“But if a serious injury results, then you must require a life for a life” (verse 23), “eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, and stripe for stripe” (verses 24-25).

If a man strikes his servant's eye and destroys it, “he must let the servant go free as compensation for the eye” (verse 26). The same is true for a tooth (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Two men are fighting, and a pregnant woman is struck. The case is about harm caused in a brawl, and the law makes the man responsible for what his violence did.

The words ‘eye for eye’ come next. They sound harsh, but they were a limit. In a world of blood feuds, a family might answer one injury with a much greater one. This rule says the penalty must fit the harm and go no further. It was given to judges, not to people taking revenge for themselves. It also applied to everyone alike. Hammurabi's law required an eye for an eye among the free, but only silver when the victim was a commoner or a slave. Leviticus says, “You are to have the same standard of law for the foreign resident and the native” (Leviticus 24:22).

Jewish tradition, in the Mishnah and the Talmud, read the rule as requiring payment equal to the injury, not literal maiming, and many scholars think it worked that way in practice.

Then the law turns the rule on its head for a servant. A master who destroys a servant's eye does not lose his own eye. He loses the servant, who goes free. Even a knocked-out tooth sets a servant free. A master's hand was limited by law.
passages.later:
‘Eye for eye’ appears three times in the law: here, in Leviticus 24:20, and in Deuteronomy 19:21. In Deuteronomy it is set in a court, where “The judges shall investigate thoroughly” (Deuteronomy 19:18).

Jesus quotes it in the Sermon on the Mount: “You have heard that it was said, ‘Eye for eye and tooth for tooth.’ But I tell you not to resist an evil person” (Matthew 5:38-39). He does not abolish it as a limit for courts. He refuses to let it rule personal wrongs, and calls his followers to give up revenge.
passages.hard:
What does verse 22 mean? The Hebrew is debated, and readers take it in two main ways.

The Hebrew says that the woman's children ‘come out’. Many read this as a birth that comes too early, with the child born alive. On this reading, ‘no further injury’ means neither mother nor child is badly hurt, and the man is fined; if either is seriously harmed, the rule of verse 23 applies. Others read it as a miscarriage, the loss of the child. On this reading, the fine is for the loss of the child, and the harsher penalty of verse 23 applies to harm done to the mother. The word for ‘serious injury’ is rare. Elsewhere it is used only of the harm Jacob feared for Benjamin (Genesis 42:4, 38; 44:29), a word for disaster.

Both readings have careful defenders. These verses are often quoted in modern debates about abortion. These notes take no political position and speak for no party or law. They set out what the Hebrew says, and how it has been read.

If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too. Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: ‘Eye for eye’ set a limit on what a court could do. Jesus asks more of his followers in their own wrongs. Ask where you keep score, and what it would mean to stop. And ask whether you want justice for others as fairly as you want it for yourself.

passages.t: An ox that gores, and an open pit
passages.happening:
“If an ox gores a man or woman to death, the ox must surely be stoned, and its meat must not be eaten. But the owner of the ox shall not be held responsible” (verse 28).

But if the ox had a habit of goring and its owner was warned and did nothing, the ox is stoned “and its owner must also be put to death” (verse 29). “If payment is demanded of him instead, he may redeem his life by paying the full amount demanded of him” (verse 30). The same rule holds if the ox gores a son or a daughter (verse 31). If it gores a servant, the owner pays the servant's master “thirty shekels of silver” (verse 32).

A man who leaves a pit open must pay for an animal that falls in (verses 33-34). If one ox kills another, the owners share the loss; but if the ox was known to be dangerous, its owner pays in full (verses 35-36).
passages.hearers:
The goring ox was a standard case in ancient law. It appears in the older Laws of Eshnunna and in Hammurabi, with the same difference between an ox with no history and one whose owner had been warned. The rule for one ox killing another in verse 35 is almost the same as a law of Eshnunna. Israel's law drew on a legal tradition shared across the region.

The difference between the first case and the second is the difference between accident and negligence. An owner is not guilty for what he could not foresee. But an owner who knew the danger and did nothing shares in the death.

The ox that kills a person is stoned, and no one may eat it. A human life was not to be treated as a loss of property. Genesis had said that God would require a reckoning for human blood, even from an animal (Genesis 9:5).

Verse 30 allows a ransom, kopher, a payment that covers a life, in place of the owner's death, because he did not intend to kill. Numbers forbids any such ransom for a murderer. The difference shows how highly the law valued a life taken on purpose.

The servant in verse 32 is still valued in silver, thirty shekels paid to the master. That is hard to read. But the ox is stoned for a servant's death just as for a free person's.
passages.later:
Thirty pieces of silver comes back in the Bible. The prophet Zechariah was paid ‘thirty pieces of silver’ and told to throw it to the potter (Zechariah 11:12-13), and Matthew says the chief priests paid Judas ‘thirty pieces of silver’ (Matthew 26:15).

The word ransom comes back too. Jesus said that he came “to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45).
passages.asks: The owner who was warned and did nothing was held responsible. Ask what danger you know about, in your home, your work or your own habits, that you have not yet dealt with. And ask whom your neglect could harm.
